concepts.definition: The process of checking that a claimed identity or origin is genuine.
concepts.falsehood: Authentication means granting permissions without checking any identity.

concepts.definition: A seal could show signs of opening and carry an impression associated with a sender.
concepts.falsehood: A wax seal mathematically proves that no forgery is possible.

concepts.definition: Visible signs that a seal or message may have been altered or opened.
concepts.falsehood: Tamper evidence guarantees that no attacker can imitate or replace a seal.

concepts.definition: A function that maps input data to a fixed-length digest for a chosen hash algorithm.
concepts.falsehood: A fixed hash algorithm must produce longer digests for longer messages.

concepts.definition: The fixed-length output of a hash function, also called a hash value or hash.
concepts.falsehood: A message digest is necessarily the original plaintext in readable form.

concepts.definition: Hashing produces a digest; encryption uses a key and is designed to be reversed by authorized parties.
concepts.falsehood: Hashing and encryption are identical reversible operations.

concepts.definition: The slide credits Hans Peter Luhn with early hashing work used to organize and search records.
concepts.falsehood: The slides describe early hashing as having no use in searching records.

concepts.definition: A group into which records can be placed to help organize lookup.
concepts.falsehood: A hash bucket is a certificate that proves a sender's identity.

concepts.definition: Historical Message Digest algorithms named in the lesson; MD5 is unsuitable where collision resistance is needed.
concepts.falsehood: MD4 and MD5 are current recommendations for new collision-resistant authentication designs.

concepts.definition: A historical cryptographic hash algorithm producing a 160-bit digest and using 80 rounds per block.
concepts.falsehood: SHA-1 produces a 512-bit digest and performs only one round per block.

concepts.definition: Families of modern hash algorithms that NIST recommends as alternatives to SHA-1.
concepts.falsehood: NIST recommends adopting SHA-1 instead of SHA-2 and SHA-3 for new collision-resistant uses.

concepts.definition: A small change in input, including a change in letter case, generally produces a different cryptographic digest.
concepts.falsehood: Changing letter case always leaves the input bytes and digest unchanged.

concepts.definition: The slide's MD5 digest for uppercase CCSICT is afa10b1e77998a5806a8b0fdff622b03.
concepts.falsehood: The slide's MD5 example says that uppercase and lowercase inputs are necessarily identical bytes.

concepts.definition: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest, commonly displayed as 32 hexadecimal characters.
concepts.falsehood: MD5's digest length grows in direct proportion to the input length.

concepts.definition: A particular hash algorithm returns the same output length even when input messages have different lengths.
concepts.falsehood: A longer message always makes MD5 return more than 128 bits.

concepts.definition: Comparing hashes of nearly identical messages illustrates that a small change can produce a very different digest.
concepts.falsehood: The same hash algorithm must output almost identical digests for nearly identical messages.

concepts.definition: Comparing a computed digest against a trusted expected digest can reveal accidental or intentional changes.
concepts.falsehood: A checksum comparison can identify changes even if an attacker can replace both the message and its expected digest.

concepts.definition: An HMAC or digital signature can protect message integrity and help authenticate the source when keys are managed correctly.
concepts.falsehood: A plain unkeyed hash sent alongside a message by itself authenticates the sender against an active attacker.

concepts.definition: MD4 stands for Message Digest 4 and is an older hash algorithm.
concepts.falsehood: MD4 is the name of a modern authentication factor rather than a hash algorithm.

concepts.definition: SHA-1 outputs 160 bits, equivalent to 20 bytes or 40 hexadecimal digits.
concepts.falsehood: SHA-1 outputs 160 hexadecimal digits for every message.

concepts.definition: SHA-1 processes padded messages in 512-bit blocks.
concepts.falsehood: SHA-1 processes a padded block containing only five bits.

concepts.definition: SHA-1 starts with five 32-bit state words, often named H0 through H4 or A through E.
concepts.falsehood: The initial SHA-1 state consists of one 512-bit word and no named working variables.

concepts.definition: A 512-bit message block is parsed into sixteen 32-bit words before the schedule is expanded.
concepts.falsehood: A 512-bit SHA-1 block is initially parsed into sixteen 64-bit words.

concepts.definition: Append a 1 bit, then zero bits, then the original message length encoded in 64 bits to reach a multiple of 512 bits.
concepts.falsehood: SHA-1 padding consists only of zeros and never includes the original message length.

concepts.definition: For t from 16 to 79, W[t] is a one-bit left rotation of W[t-3] XOR W[t-8] XOR W[t-14] XOR W[t-16].
concepts.falsehood: SHA-1 expands W[t] using W[t-13] in place of W[t-3].

concepts.definition: The round function changes across four 20-round ranges; the first uses (B AND C) OR ((NOT B) AND D).
concepts.falsehood: The first SHA-1 round function omits NOT B from its second term.

concepts.definition: Each of four SHA-1 round ranges uses a specified constant, beginning with 5a827999 for rounds 0–19.
concepts.falsehood: Every SHA-1 round uses the same constant regardless of its range.

concepts.definition: The lecture's printed schedule and first-round function contain typos; use the standard formulas in the explanation.
concepts.falsehood: Every formula and range printed on the lecture's SHA-1 properties slide is error-free.

concepts.falsehood: The sample's encoded length word 00000028 represents 28 decimal bits.

concepts.definition: In the first round, the old A becomes new B and rotating the old B left by 30 bits gives new C.
concepts.falsehood: In a SHA-1 round, the previous A is discarded without affecting any new state word.

concepts.definition: A rotate-left moves bits around a fixed 32-bit word, wrapping the bits that leave the left end back to the right.
concepts.falsehood: A 32-bit rotate-left permanently discards all bits shifted out of the word.

concepts.definition: Rotating efcdab89 left by 30 bits produces 7bf36ae2.
concepts.falsehood: Rotating efcdab89 left by 30 bits produces 00000000.

concepts.falsehood: SHA-1 is recommended for new digital signatures because it is collision resistant.

title: Avalanche Effect Computation
subtitle: Compare ciphertext bits and interpret the result

concepts.definition: Assessing how well an algorithm resists attacks and protects data, considering evidence such as cryptanalysis and performance.
concepts.falsehood: A single runtime measurement completely proves an algorithm is secure.

concepts.definition: The time required to perform an operation; it is a performance consideration distinct from security strength.
concepts.falsehood: A faster algorithm is automatically more secure than every slower algorithm.

concepts.definition: A property where a small input change can cause a substantial, unpredictable change in a cryptographic output.
concepts.falsehood: The avalanche effect means every output bit remains unchanged after any input bit changes.

concepts.definition: Flipping one input bit is a common controlled way to study the avalanche effect.
concepts.falsehood: A controlled avalanche test must change every input bit at once.

concepts.definition: The encrypted output produced by an encryption algorithm under a particular key and configuration.
concepts.falsehood: Ciphertext is the original unencrypted message by definition.

concepts.definition: A symmetric-key block cipher with a 64-bit block size; the lesson uses it as an example for comparison.
concepts.falsehood: Blowfish has a 128-bit block size.

concepts.definition: Compare outputs from the same algorithm and key with settings held constant while changing the intended input bit.
concepts.falsehood: A fair avalanche experiment should change the input, key, mode, and IV all at once.

concepts.definition: To reproduce encrypted output, specify the key, mode, IV or nonce when applicable, encoding, and padding.
concepts.falsehood: Knowing only a plaintext and the algorithm name always determines a unique ciphertext.

concepts.definition: In ASCII-compatible encoding, uppercase I and lowercase i differ by one bit: 0x49 XOR 0x69 equals 0x20.
concepts.falsehood: ASCII uppercase I and lowercase i differ in every bit of their byte values.

concepts.definition: One hexadecimal digit represents four bits, so 32 hexadecimal digits represent 128 bits.
concepts.falsehood: A hexadecimal digit represents exactly one bit.

concepts.definition: XOR corresponding output bits; the 1 bits in the result mark positions where the outputs differ.
concepts.falsehood: XOR produces a 1 when the two corresponding input bits are equal.

concepts.definition: The number of bit positions at which two equal-length bit strings differ.
